title: How to Build a Sovereign Global Knowledge Commons | Katina Magazine
content: "Scholarly publishing has its own potential single points of failure. The indexing databases, hosting platforms, and citation infrastructures of the Western scholarly record are concentrated among a small number of commercial owners, each exposed to the same risk. The point is not that a change of ownership at a scholarly publisher would make headlines like the Twitter takeover did. It is that the underlying structural condition—a single point of control over infrastructure that many depend on and few govern—is the same, and that the appropriate response is also the same: distribute governance and control rights before the acquisition or the political pressure occurs, not after."

title: Recommendations for Revising the Open Access Classification System in OpenAlex | Zenodo
content: "The open access (OA) color classification system used by Unpaywall (i.e., Gold, Green, Hybrid, Bronze, and closed) was introduced in 2018 and has since become widely used across the ecosystem, including by Scopus, Web of Science, Dimensions, and numerous funders and institutions worldwide. However, the scholarly communication landscape has changed significantly since these categories were defined and the limits of this system are proving problematic. In particular, the current system struggles with research outputs that are not journal publications, relies too heavily on journal-level policies rather than work-level attributes, conflates business models with access status, and is difficult to accurately operationalize in an environment where journals regularly change the OA status of publications en masse. The OpenAlex Colors Working Group was convened by the OpenAlex Community Advisory Board in January 2026 to evaluate these limitations and recommend a revised framework. title: Biomedical Publishing Metrics as a Barrier to Knowledge Dissemination
content: Abstract:  The Journal Impact Factor (JIF) is an outdated biomedical metric that hinders knowledge dissemination. Relying on citation counts creates a skewed, easily manipulated system with a temporal lag that ignores global equity. Frontline clinicians consume research to improve care but rarely generate citations, meaning the JIF cannot capture real-world clinical utility. To ensure rankings reflect true value, publishers must adopt a multi-dimensional matrix prioritizing usage-based Altmetrics, such as verified downloads and views, to instantly measure global clinical application.

title: Unlocking knowledge: diamond open access publishing - UNESCO Digital Library
content: Diamond Open Access (OA) is an equitable scholarly publishing model that treats knowledge as a digital public good, with no fees for readers or authors. Built on shared infrastructure, open licensing, and community governance, it supports non-profit, academically driven publishing while allowing commercial providers to deliver specific services. Like Open Educational Resources (OER), Diamond OA promotes equitable access, collaboration, and multilingual knowledge sharing. It can strengthen national and institutional Open Access strategies while connecting OER, Open Data, and open research software into interoperable knowledge ecosystems. This brief examines Diamond OA infrastructure and provides practical policy guidance for Member States and institutions.

title: From access to impact: the gold OA advantage | Springer Nature
content:
"This white paper explores the effect of different routes to OA on the reach and impact of articles in hybrid journals. The data shows that, 8 years on from our first major study into this topic, there is still a substantial advantage for gold OA articles across all disciplines (measured by downloads, citations and Altmetric Attention Score) over both non-OA articles and green OA articles. 4

The analysis of 204,781 articles published in 1,812 hybrid Springer Nature journals in 2023 also shows how gold OA can accelerate the number of downloads over time and the diversity of geographic readership, leading to faster impact and greater equity in access."

title: Open Access Library and Information Science (LIS) Journals Indexed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ): An Analytical Study | Annals of Library and Information Studies
content: Abstract: The study examines the trends and current status of Open Access (OA) research journals listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) in the field of Library and Information Science (LIS) from 2003 to mid-2026. It investigates the profile of OA LIS journals, publishing trends, publishing practices, open access policies, licensing practices and journal scope through thematic analysis of keywords. The study identified 231 OA LIS journals published in 32 languages by 200 publishers across 55 countries globally. The study adopted a descriptive research approach and data were collected from the DOAJ and verified through the official journal websites where required. The collected data were compiled, organised, tabulated and analysed using Microsoft Excel. The findings provide insights into the growth of LIS journals, geographical distribution, publishers, language profile, publication mode, peer-review practices, article processing charges (APCs), copyright ownership, Creative Commons licensing, self-archiving policies, digital preservation mechanisms, Digital Object Identifier (DOI) availability and other publishing infrastructure adopted by OA LIS journals.

The population consisted of 227 postgraduate students from five universities: Adeleke University (AU) - 22, Babcock University (BU)-35, Lead City University (LCU)-30, Tai Solarin University (TASUED)-30 and University of Ibadan (UI)-110. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire administered through the total enumeration technique. The collected data were analysed using both descriptive and inferential statistical methods. The findings revealed that the largest respondents were: UI (49%), females (50.7%), age group 26-30 (39.4%), and single (55.9%). OARs were used mostly for research work (=3.60); group/individual practical purposes (=3.34) personal tutorials (=3.26) and examination preparation (=3.24). title: Strengthening Trust and Leadership: Reflections on National Institutes of Health (NIH) 2026 Community Days: Securing NIH Controlled-Access Data and Our Data Protection Journey | Data Science at NIH
content: "On April 13 and 14, I had the privilege of leading the National Institutes of Health (NIH) 2026 Community Days: Securing NIH Controlled-Access Data webinars to engage directly with our stakeholders, researchers, and the broader public about the critical work we’re undertaking to protect controlled-access data. These sessions were designed to foster transparency around our security and operational standards, update the community on new resources and requirements, and reinforce our shared responsibility in safeguarding participant trust. I am deeply grateful for the vibrant participation and thoughtful questions that were raised, which underscores the importance and urgency of our mission. Protecting participants’ trust requires one standard: secure, consistent protections for NIH controlled-access data—whether it is processed within a NIH Controlled-Access Data Repository (CADR) or a research institution’s IT systems. This principle drove the Extramural Community Days agenda, where we discussed not only what needs to be done, but why rigorous data protection is more essential than ever. title: New UKRN reports highlight opportunities and limits of AI-powered monitoring of research data sharing | UK Reproducibility Network
content: "Two new reports from the UKRN – Working Paper 13: Monitoring Data Availability Statements and FAIR Data Practices in Medical Research Council (MRC)-Funded Research and UKRN Working Paper 14: Monitoring Data Sharing and FAIR Practices with LLMs – provide fresh evidence on how research funders and institutions can monitor data-sharing practices at scale, and what role artificial intelligence is likely to play in the future. Together, the reports address a growing challenge for research policy: how to assess whether publicly funded research data can be found, accessed and reused without relying on costly manual review of thousands of publications every year. While expectations around open research and FAIR data have become increasingly widespread, robust monitoring remains difficult. The first report examines a sample of 2023 publications acknowledging support from the Medical Research Council (MRC). It found that Data Availability Statements (DASs) were present in more than 80% of publications, but only around 59% were judged acceptable against established criteria. The study also identified practical problems that affect discoverability, including non-resolving dataset identifiers

title: Popular open-science platform to stop hosting data and code amid funding concerns | Nature
content:
"The co-founder of a prominent open-science platform has announced that funding uncertainties have forced the site to make changes to some of its most popular features.

In a statement released on 11 August, Brian Nosek, executive director of the Center for Open Science (COS) in Charlottesville, Virginia, which runs the Open Science Framework (OSF), announced that the platform will no longer allow researchers to post their code and data after 16 November. Any documents that are already publicly available on the site will remain online. But users will no longer be able to upload new materials in private mode.

The OSF’s preregistration workflow — which allows scientists to post research designs and articles that describe their planned methods and analyses for upcoming experiments — will continue to operate as normal, as will the 14 preprint servers run on the OSF platform."

title: Frontiers | Does Interdisciplinary Breadth Shape Research Data Sharing and Citation Impact? Evidence from Six Research Fields
content: Abstract: Research data sharing has become an important component of open science, yet sharing benefits vary across research contexts. Existing studies have examined factors influencing data sharing and the citation advantage associated with open data, but less is known about how interdisciplinary breadth relates to observable sharing practices and whether the citation advantage of sharing differs across disciplines. This study investigates the relationships among interdisciplinary breadth, observable sharing practices, and citation impact using 566,188 journal articles indexed in OpenAlex from 2020 to 2025. Interdisciplinary breadth was operationalized as the number of Level-0 disciplinary concepts associated with each article. Observable sharing practices were identified through repository links, supplementary-material links, and textual sharing statements. Regression models were applied to examine associations among interdisciplinary breadth, data sharing, and citation impact across six research fields, and BERTopic-based topic modeling was also applied in history and digital humanities to explore topic-level variations. title: Kirsch | Assessing Researcher Data Sharing Practices Using Publicly Available Dataset Metadata: A Reproducible Workflow for Institutional Stakeholders | Journal of Librarianship and Scholarly Communication
content: Abstract: Introduction: Scholarly communities are experiencing increased emphasis on research data sharing and reuse. Given the range of available data repositories and variability in the use of persistent identifiers (PIDs) for individuals and institutions, aggregating datasets by researchers at a specific institution is a significant challenge. We developed a reproducible workflow to evaluate 1) data repository use by researchers at our institutions, 2) metrics of reuse, and 3) quality of metadata records. Methods: We used the DataCite REST API to locate metadata records for datasets with creator affiliation names that matched our institutions. We performed substantial cleaning and deduplication before comparing repository use, citations, usage metrics, and metadata completeness. Results: The most common data repositories were Dryad, Harvard Dataverse, figshare, Zenodo, ICPSR, and one institution’s institutional repository. title: Wiley research publishing revenue jumps 12pc on OA growth and Emerald acquisition - Research Information
content:
"Wiley has reported 4% growth in its research division for the first quarter of its 2027 financial year, with publishing revenue climbing 12% as strong demand for open access and the addition of Emerald Publishing boosted the business.

Research revenue reached $293 million for the three months ended 31 July 2026, up 4% both on a reported basis and at constant currency.

Research Publishing revenue increased 12% at constant currency, driven by what Wiley described as strong growth in gold open access and AI licensing, alongside a $13 million contribution from Emerald Publishing following completion of the acquisition during the quarter.

The performance helped offset a 30% decline in Research Solutions revenue, which faced a tough comparison with the same period last year because of AI licensing income. Research Solutions generated $4 million in AI licensing revenue during the quarter, compared with $16 million a year earlier."

title: Six UK universities renew unlimited open access deal with JMIR Publications - Research Information
content:
"Six UK universities have renewed an unlimited open access publishing agreement with JMIR Publications through Jisc, extending the arrangement until July 2027.

Newcastle University, the University of Leeds, University of Manchester, University of Nottingham, University of Southampton and University of Warwick have renewed their participation in JMIR Publications’ Flat-Fee Unlimited Open Access Publishing Agreement.

The model replaces individual article processing charges (APCs) with an institutional publishing subscription, allowing eligible researchers at participating universities to publish without paying an APC.

Corresponding authors affiliated with the six institutions can publish across JMIR Publications’ portfolio of more than 30 Gold Open Access journals, covering research across the digital health sector. The renewed agreement runs until 31 July 2027.

JMIR said the subscription model is designed to reduce the administrative and financial barriers associated with individual APC payments, while giving institutions greater predictability over their open access publishing costs."

title: Project MUSE - The Data Rescue Project: A Crowdsourced Effort to Preserve At-Risk US Federal Data
content: Abstract: The US federal government is the world's largest data publisher. Since Trump's second inauguration, these data are threatened because their scope contravenes regime ideology and the offices that maintain these datasets no longer have adequate staff to preserve and provide access to the data. The Data Rescue Project was launched in 2025 as a community response to this crisis. We organized volunteers to work on data rescues, focusing especially on social data to fill an identified gap in other rescue efforts and emphasizing curation of the datasets for long-term data preservation. Through community-building, we became a coordinating body for the data rescue movement, streamlining communication and preventing duplication of effort in the US and internationally. In this article, we use the Data Rescue Project as a case study on building coalitions to push back against the destruction of digital information. Moreover, the US is not unique in its need for these efforts. content: "The 3-D digitization will take pictures all around the object and process them, using a photogrammetric procedure which identifies common features in the different images. The process orients the images in space and then performs what’s called the calibration of the camera, Guidi said. Once these steps are completed, image matching will automatically generate a dense cloud of 3-D points. This leads to generating the mesh, which is the model, the shape of the object, and its texture, he said. “You have to take several photographs around the object, and then you merge them and you process them in such a way…(that) gives you a digital twin of the physical object,” he said. “A digital twin means that also the size is totally the same, so it can be measured and analyzed, and this is very useful if you want to study something.” Possible challenges will be digitizing shiny or transparent objects because they are not compatible with the optical process used to generate the model. content: "This blog post argues that the next stage of AI evolution should move beyond isolated open initiatives toward Open AI Infrastructure: a systems architecture that integrates open models, open compute, open networking, and open orchestration into an interoperable execution fabric. Rather than proposing another initiative, Open AI Infrastructure provides the architectural framework that enables existing initiatives to operate together as a distributed intelligent system."

title: Altmetrics and Traditional Citation Impact among Top Iranian Researchers: A Comparative Analysis of ResearchGate and Academia
content: Abstract: Objective: The rapid expansion of digital communication has introduced alternative indicators of research visibility and impact, transforming traditional scholarly evaluation. This study investigates the potential of academic social networks for assessing the scholarly impact of Iranian researchers through an altmetrics approach. Method: This study employed a quantitative, cross-sectional design focused on the top 1% of Iranian researchers, as identified by the Islamic World Science Citation Center (ISC). Using a stratified sampling method, a sample of 203 researchers was selected across diverse disciplines. Data were collected between June 22, 2025, and June 4, 2026, by retrieving article-level metrics from Scopus, ResearchGate, and Academia.edu. Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient was applied to examine the relationship between Scopus citation counts and platform-specific engagement indicators (reads and views). Results: The analysis revealed a statistically significant positive correlation between Scopus citations and ResearchGate reads (r = 0.525). title: Power, Equity, and the Future of Open - SPARC
content: "Building on our popular “Open Access 101” events, SPARC is pleased to announce a new series, Collections & Open Access: Resourcing Open Scholarship, that will dive deeper into topics at the intersection of library collections and Open Access. This series will examine how collections librarians are navigating major changes, including funder public access requirements and evolving publisher business models, and consider what these changes mean for the future of libraries. The series will explore broader trends in the evolution of collections work, the practical realities of how different libraries are approaching these changes, and what lessons other institutions might draw from their experience. Resourcing Open Access is a three-part webinar series designed for collections-focused librarians and others engaged in this work. Together, we will move from foundational concepts to implementation to critical reflection—exploring not only how this work gets done, but why it matters and for whom. title: Available: OA Switchboard plugin for OJS 3.5 | OA Switchboard
content:
Supporting Diamond journals in increasing the visibility of their open access output among research funders, institutions and consortia.

The integration plugin connecting Open Journal Systems (OJS) with the OA Switchboard is now compatible with OJS 3.5.0.x. Journals running OJS 3.5 can start using the plugin right away.

Once enabled, the plugin automatically sends a set of public article metadata to relevant research funders and institutions via the OA Switchboard when an article is published. The metadata is captured at the point of publication and shared with the institutions affiliated with the article’s authors and the funders supporting the underlying research.

This happens automatically, with no additional manual work required from the editorial team, helping diamond open access journals make their published research more visible to the organisations that fund and support it.

content:
"HathiTrust has been awarded a five-year, $5 million grant for Transparent Books: AI Infrastructure for Discovery and the Public Interest from the Mellon Foundation. Authors Alliance is a partner in the project alongside Northeastern University Library. 

For us, this grant continues work we began with the Public Interest Corpus: opening a path for research libraries to lawfully make the books in their collections usable for computational research and discovery on terms that support the goals of research, scholarship and access to knowledge, rather than on terms that benefit commercial intermediaries and technology companies."
